HPS is a group of ten autosomal recessive disorders, defined by a deficiency of specific genes, each of which encodes a component of four ubiquitantly expressed protein complexes: AP‐3 and biogenesis of the lysosome‐related organella complex (BLOC)‐1 through ‐3.

HPS is a group of ten autosomal recessive disorders, each defined as a deficiency of one of the ten genes, and that the HPS‐related genes encode components of ubiquitously expressed four protein complexes.
HPS is a group of autosomal recessive, multisystem disorders, with 10 genes identified.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for HPS.
the identification of genetic factors involved in the pathophysiology of human disease.
the molecular genetics of Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (HP) and related diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the clinical and cellular features of HPS are highly variable depending on the defective gene and its function in a specific protein complex.
the molecular diagnosis of HPS should be considered in patients presenting with albinism and/or a bleeding diatheses and/or other symptoms of HPS.
the HPS gene mutations are highly diverse and the disease phenotype is highly variable, which makes it a challenge to diagnose and treat HPS patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HPS is a rare genetic disorder that affects many systems of the human body.
10 HPS‐associated gene defects have been identified to date, and that the HPS‐associated proteins are involved in the biogenesis of lysosomes and lysosome‐related membrane compartments.
HPS is a clinically heterogeneous group of diseases, with the most frequent subtypes being BLOC‐2 and BLOC‐1 deficiency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HPS is not rare, but the number of reported cases is still low, and that the majority of cases remain unidentified.
HPS‐associated variants are highly diverse and that the pathogenicity of missense and splice variants is not always predictable.
HPS should be considered as differential diagnosis in all patients with albinism or a bleeding diatheses and that molecular diagnosis is essential for accurate clinical management and prognosis.
